tldr: This survey paper formalizes the "embodiment gap"—the remaining adaptation effort required before running a robot foundation model on a new physical robot—and proposes a framework to report and compare real-robot adaptation costs that success rates alone conceal.
overview:
In recent years, research on robot foundation models (RFMs) and vision-language-action (VLA) models has surged, aiming for generalization by scaling up data and model sizes. However, unlike language or images, robots operate through physical bodies. Even when a model generalizes, extensive hands-on engineering—such as calibration, controller tuning, and refining contact dynamics—remains indispensable before it can run on a specific target robot. The authors define this gap between reusable structures and real execution on a target robot as the embodiment gap.

Existing studies are often evaluated purely on final task success rate. Yet achieving the same success rate with minimal adjustment has vastly different practical value than achieving it through days of human intervention and manual resets. To address this, the authors organize diverse existing methods on a two-axis map: what is shared across embodiments (semantics, perception, actions, morphology, etc.) versus where the remaining adaptation work lies (control interface alignment, contact and force control, etc.). They also categorize recent approaches into three research directions (sharing semantics and perception, sharing robot data and interfaces, and learning correspondence across embodiments), clarifying the strengths and limitations of each.

Furthermore, the paper proposes a "minimum report card" to objectively record adaptation work hidden behind success rates, as well as the "Embodiment Adaptation Curve (EAC)" to plot adaptation effort against performance. This survey serves as an essential guide for future RFM development, shedding light on what scaling laws alone can solve and what engineering challenges remain on the physical body.
contributions: Clearly defining the embodiment gap as the divide between reusable models, representations, or data and real-robot execution on a target robot.

Qualitatively positioning existing foundation models and datasets on a two-axis map spanning shared structure versus remaining work stages, while analyzing the strengths and limits of three major research directions.
Proposing a reporting framework (the minimum report card and the Embodiment Adaptation Curve) to visualize and compare the adaptation effort and failure modes hidden behind task success rates alone.

sections.heading: In the Era of Large Models, Why Does the "Physical Body" Remain a Barrier for Robots?
sections.summary: Scaling laws that revolutionized language and vision are spreading to robotics, but robots can act only through specific physical bodies. This section emphasizes the embodiment gap between model reusability and execution, highlighting why adaptation effort matters just as much as task success rates.
sections.details:
The scaling hypothesis—that larger models and more data yield generalization—has swept through NLP and computer vision, and it is rapidly permeating robotics through robot foundation models (RFMs) and VLA policies like RT-X, Octo, OpenVLA, and $\pi_{0}$. Yet robotics has a crucial difference: no matter how broadly a shared model is pre-trained, it cannot produce physical motion on real motors out of the box.

Translating shared models or representations into actionable motor commands on a specific target robot requires substantial effort, including controller tuning and safety verification. The authors term this divide the embodiment gap. In industrial robotics, this invisible work has historically been handled by system integrators using tacit knowledge and hard-won experience. The exact same challenge arises with modern foundation models.

Currently, most papers evaluate policies solely on final task success rates. But an 80% success rate achieved zero-shot means something completely different from an 80% success rate reached after hundreds of human interventions and manual adjustments. This survey organizes existing work into three research directions to clarify what can be resolved by scaling models and data, and what remains as engineering effort on the target platform.

sections.heading: What Exactly Is the Embodiment Gap? Drawing the Line with Related Concepts
sections.summary: This section operationalizes the embodiment gap and distinguishes it from neighboring concepts like domain shift and general system integration. The core test is whether the extra work stems from changing the robot's physical body.
sections.details:
2.1 Operational Definition:
In this paper, the embodiment gap is defined as the gap that arises when models, representations, or data shared across multiple robots are translated into executable actions matching the morphology and control system of a target robot. The central question is whether switching embodiments introduces additional adaptation work on the target platform. Shared structures can sit far from execution (like task semantics or abstract plans) or closer to execution (like action spaces and motor skills).

2.2 Relationship to Neighboring Concepts:
The practical test to determine what falls inside the embodiment gap is whether the challenge is caused by differences in physical bodies.
- Variations in lighting or object appearance on the same robot constitute domain shifts, while learning a new procedure is task adaptation. Because the robot body does not change, these are outside the primary scope of the embodiment gap.
- In contrast, retuning controllers and action spaces when transferring a policy to a new arm, or redesigning grasp patterns because a hand has a different number of fingers for the same cup-lifting task, are textbook examples of the embodiment gap.
- Moreover, out of general hardware setup tasks (such as cable routing), the embodiment gap covers the adjustments and recovery mechanisms needed to execute shared models safely and reliably on the new robot. It encompasses the entire process of making physical behavior succeed, not just matching end-effector command formats.

sections.heading: A Two-Axis Map of Existing Methods: What We Share vs. What Work Remains
sections.summary: The authors classify 21 representative method groups on a two-axis map comparing the distance of shared structure from execution against the remaining stage of target adaptation. This visually exposes what each approach scales and where it leaves manual effort.
sections.details:
3.1 Constructing the Two-Axis Map:
To compare existing methods, the authors establish two qualitative axes:
- Horizontal axis (shared structure): Indicates how far the shared representation is from physical execution on the target robot. Moving from left to right: Semantics and Tasks (planning) $\to$ Perception and Affordances (where to act) $\to$ Object Interactions (how objects should move) $\to$ Actions and Skills (trajectories and low-level commands) $\to$ Morphology-Aware Sharing (explicit robot kinematics/joint layouts).
- Vertical axis (remaining work): Indicates the primary stage of adaptation left on the target robot. Moving from top to bottom: Task-to-Skill Connection (linking plans to skills) $\to$ Calibration and Control Interface Alignment (matching outputs to robot controllers) $\to$ Contact and Force Control Execution (sustaining contact and correcting deviations) $\to$ Safety and Recovery (handling faults, retries, and resets).

3.2 Qualitative Map of Existing Work:
Three researchers independently coded 21 representative method groups. The horizontal axis showed high agreement (76.2% full agreement across three coders, Fleiss' $\kappa = 0.78$). In contrast, distinguishing between control interface alignment and contact/force control on the vertical axis proved harder, yielding $\kappa = 0.33$. After applying priority rules to resolve ties, the map revealed that as shared structure moves closer to execution, remaining work also shifts closer to physical execution. Notably, zero methods were categorized under the Safety and Recovery row. This exposes a blind spot in current foundation model research: almost all effort focuses on task achievement, leaving fault tolerance and autonomous recovery neglected in core designs.

3.3 Three Scaling Directions:
Existing methods broadly divide into three approaches:
- (1) Sharing Semantics and Perception: Leverages massive web data for broad generalization, but leaves the entire conversion into physical action to downstream engineering.
- (2) Sharing Robot Data and Interfaces: Uses real robot data to sit closer to execution, but suffers from high data collection costs and still requires contact and controller tuning.
- (3) Learning Correspondence Across Embodiments: A promising path that absorbs hardware differences inside the model, though scaling its representations and data remains in early stages.

sections.heading: Direction 1: Sharing Semantics and Perception — Bringing Web-Scale Knowledge to the Physical World
sections.summary: This group of methods leverages large language and vision models to share task plans and spatial affordances across robots. While benefitting from web-scale pre-training, connecting plans to executable skills and stabilizing physical contact still demands separate engineering.
sections.details:
This direction brings the power of foundation models pre-trained on massive internet text, images, and videos into robotics. Its biggest advantage is reusing high-level reasoning—deciding what to do and where to look—without training each robot from scratch.

- Semantics and Task Level: Planning frameworks using SayCan or various LLMs decompose high-level tasks and select candidate actions. However, executing an LLM-generated plan requires the target robot to already possess reliable low-level skills. If a required skill is missing, even a flawless plan cannot run.
- Perception and Affordance Level: Methods such as CLIPort, PerAct, and VoxPoser ground language in visual scenes to output spatial affordances indicating where to interact. Yet these outputs only highlight contact locations. They do not dictate how to approach or sustain contact given differences in arm reach or gripper geometry.
- Video and World Models: Models predicting dynamic scene changes (video prediction and imitation learning) represent how objects should move over time, bringing representations closer to execution. However, tracking those desired changes via real-robot closed-loop control and correcting for contact slippage remain unresolved engineering burdens.
- VLA Policies: Modern models like OpenVLA and $\pi_{0}$ combine vision-language models with multi-robot real execution data to predict actions directly. Nevertheless, their action spaces remain tied to the control frequencies and coordinate systems of the training data. In practice, downstream fine-tuning on the target platform to adjust speeds and scaling is almost always necessary.

sections.heading: Direction 2: Sharing Robot Data and Interfaces — The Promise and Limits of Standardization
sections.summary: This approach aims to scale physical robot learning by adopting common data schemas, hardware interfaces, and action representations. While it builds a crucial foundation for scaling, standardizing software commands does not eliminate discrepancies in physical contact dynamics across different hardware.
sections.details:
Collecting physical robot data is vastly more laborious than gathering web text or images. This direction seeks to standardize robot setups, teleoperation hardware, and action representations so that community-collected data can train shared models.

- Datasets and Infrastructure: Datasets like BridgeData V2, Open X-Embodiment (OXE), DROID, and LeRobot enable multi-robot data sharing using unified formats such as RLDS. However, even in public datasets, metadata quality varies widely—such as control frequencies, camera geometry, and whether actions are joint angles or end-effector poses. This makes diagnosing transfer failures on new setups difficult.
- Teleoperation and Common Interfaces: Systems like ALOHA for low-cost bimanual teleoperation and UMI for handheld gripper demonstrations standardize capture formats to collect large volumes of high-quality data. But replaying recorded end-effector trajectories on a different arm or gripper often leads to kinematic singularities or dropped grasps due to altered contact forces.
- Action Representations and Normalization: Adopting task frames, object-centric frames, SE(3) representations, or equivariant policies reduces the impact of differing robot base placements. However, sharing an action format provides no guarantee that a "move forward 1 cm" command will yield identical contact forces or friction on different robots. In contact-rich tasks, this discrepancy dictates success or failure.
- Trajectory Generation Policies (e.g., Diffusion Policy): While diffusion policies excel at modeling multimodal trajectory distributions smoothly, minor shifts in camera viewpoints or robot dynamics can destabilize physical contact, even if the trajectory appears visually clean.

sections.heading: Direction 3: Learning Cross-Embodiment Correspondence — Teaching Models to Bridge Physical Differences
sections.summary: Rather than relying solely on external tuning, this direction trains models to learn mappings between different robot bodies. Researchers explore correspondences across object motions, latent actions, kinematic morphology, and tactile/force feedback.
sections.details:
This ambitious direction tackles embodiment differences by having models learn the correspondences between different robots directly, rather than relying on external engineering.

- High-Level and Intermediate Correspondence: Methods like XSkill use abstract skill spaces, while frameworks like Track2Act leverage 2D/3D point tracking and flow. Sharing "how the object should move" abstracts away hardware differences, but target robots still require distinct low-level policies to grasp and apply force. Similarly, MOTIF extracts latent action motifs to facilitate few-shot transfer.
- Morphology-Aware Models: Architectures like Body Transformer, GET-Zero, X-VLA, and RodriNet explicitly feed robot kinematic trees and joint configurations into the network. This resolves geometric motion discrepancies across arms with different reach and degrees of freedom. However, knowing kinematics does not capture contact friction on rubber fingerpads or motor backlash, leaving contact slip and disturbance recovery unsolved.
- Integrating Tactile and Force Sensing: To observe contact discrepancies that vision misses, works like TactAlign and Tactile-VLA integrate touch and force sensing. Tactile feedback provides powerful closed-loop compensation for body differences. At the same time, differences in sensor geometries and mounting introduce a new embodiment gap, making tactile standardization and transfer the next hurdle.
- Paired and Correspondence Datasets: Datasets pairing human hands with robot grippers (like UMI and DexCap) or recording identical tasks across multiple robots (like Polybot) are growing. They provide crucial grounding data for models to learn true cross-body correspondences.

sections.heading: Beyond Raw Success Rates: A Framework to Expose the True Adaptation Process
sections.summary: The authors introduce a "minimum report card" to document hidden adaptation work, the Embodiment Adaptation Curve (EAC) to track performance against adaptation cost, and a 4-part taxonomy to diagnose real-robot failure modes.
sections.details:
7.1 Minimum Report Card:
The proposed report card (Table 1) asks researchers to document source-to-target hardware differences, shared structures, modified model components (heads vs. full backbone), target data volume, calibration and tuning time, human interventions or safety stops during evaluation, and the breakdown of failure modes across evaluation trials.
When auditing nine influential papers against this standard (Table 2), seven did not report intervention or recovery counts at all, and three left calibration and setup details unclear. Without this context, external researchers cannot tell whether high success rates reflect autonomous model generalization or extensive manual babysitting.

7.2 Embodiment Adaptation Curve (EAC):
Borrowing from machine learning scaling curves, the EAC plots task success rate on the vertical axis against the adaptation effort invested on the target robot (demonstrations collected, real-world trials, human interventions) on the horizontal axis (Figure 4). This curve visually separates policies that jump to high performance with a handful of demonstrations from those requiring hundreds of trial-and-error runs, enabling fair comparisons of transfer efficiency.

7.3 Four-Part Failure Taxonomy:
Instead of lumping unsuccessful runs into a single "failure" metric, the authors categorize failures to identify bottlenecks:
- (1) Semantics and Perception Failures (misinterpreting instructions, missing objects)
- (2) Robot Data and Interface Failures (mismatched command formats or control frequencies)
- (3) Cross-Embodiment Correspondence Failures (demanding out-of-reach poses, unachievable trajectory tracking)
- (4) Target Execution Failures (contact slipping, improper force exertion, unrecoverable states)
This taxonomy clarifies whether researchers need to improve model reasoning or re-engineer low-level control and contact interfaces.

sections.heading: Four Recommendations to Truly Bridge the Physical Divide
sections.summary: The survey outlines four priority directions for future scaling: logging the adaptation process itself, designing RFMs as adaptive systems, sharing multimodal contact dynamics including touch, and establishing evaluation benchmarks that account for human effort.
sections.details:
Synthesizing their analysis, the authors propose four focal areas for future robot foundation model research:

1. Record the Adaptation Process as Data, Not Just Expert Trajectories:
Current datasets almost exclusively feature pristine, successful trajectories. Communities should instead record the calibration logs, contact retries, and recovery behaviors humans perform when deploying a robot. Training models on these adaptation trajectories can teach RFMs how to adapt to unfamiliar hardware autonomously.

2. Design RFMs as Adaptive Systems:
Rather than relying purely on end-to-end action outputs, RFMs should incorporate supervisory agents that diagnose frequency and kinematic mismatches, selecting and tuning downstream controllers accordingly. Safe stops and autonomous resets must become core architecture components rather than ad-hoc safety overrides.

3. Turn Contact-Rich Physical Interactions into Shared Structures:
Robot learning must advance beyond kinematic geometry to learn multimodal representations that incorporate force, tactile, and audio feedback. Rich representations pre-trained on sensor-packed robots can then be inferred or distilled onto sparsely-sensed platforms to facilitate contact-rich manipulation transfer.

4. Embed Adaptation Effort into Evaluation Benchmarks:
Robotics benchmarks must move past isolated success rates. Standard metrics should jointly report target-domain data requirements, human intervention counts, and hardware tuning time, rewarding models that deploy with minimal practical friction.

sections.heading: Conclusion: From Action Generators to Physically Adaptive Robot Systems
sections.summary: The survey concludes by summarizing the embodiment gap and reiterating that conquering it requires expanding beyond web-scale semantic knowledge into system-level integration of contact dynamics and autonomous recovery.
sections.details:
This paper formalized the embodiment gap—the work remaining before a robot foundation model can execute tasks on an unfamiliar body—and surveyed current approaches. While the three scaling directions (semantics/perception, data/interfaces, and correspondence learning) have broadened reusability, bridging the final mile still depends heavily on manual engineering: aligning controllers, stabilizing contact forces, and recovering from failures safely.

Scaling laws in robotics cannot rely on expanding information-space knowledge alone; they must model physical interaction and real-world adaptation through physical bodies. The two-axis map, report card, and EAC framework introduced here provide a compass to guide the field from brittle action-generation models toward robust systems that autonomously adapt to new bodies in the physical world.

sections.heading: Appendix: Literature Selection, Boundary Conditions, and Coding Procedures
sections.summary: The appendix details paper selection criteria, boundary lines with adjacent fields, independent coding protocols and inter-rater agreement across three researchers, and a sample report card filled out for OpenVLA.
sections.details:
The appendix outlines the operational procedures ensuring survey objectivity and reproducibility:
- Literature Selection Policy (Appendix A): Focusing on manipulation, the authors collected major RFM, VLA, cross-embodiment learning, teleoperation, tactile sensing, and benchmarking papers and preprints up to early 2026, prioritizing representative models and explicit correspondence methods.
- Boundary Conditions with Related Concepts (Appendix B): The authors strictly excluded appearance-only domain shifts and routine task adaptations that do not stem from physical body differences, keeping the focus squarely on embodiment changes.
- Coding and Decision Rules (Appendix C): Three researchers independently coded 21 method groups. Because the boundary between control interface alignment and contact/force control proved ambiguous on the vertical axis, explicit priority rules were established: prioritize control interface alignment if new training or decoders are needed; prioritize contact/force control if actions are already mapped but contact dynamics and closed-loop corrections remain the primary issue.
- Sample Report Card (Appendix D): The authors fill out the minimum report card for OpenVLA, showing which metrics can be extracted directly and which remain "Not Reported (N/R)" (such as intervention counts and specific setup times), offering a practical checklist for future research reporting.

takeaways: When reading robot foundation model papers, look beyond reported task success rates and scrutinize how much hardware tuning, target data collection, and human intervention were needed to achieve them.

Current methods successfully share semantics and kinematic trajectories, but the core physical execution layers—calibrating contact forces, correcting slip, and safe autonomous recovery—remain largely unaddressed frontiers.
Adopt the habit of visualizing adaptation cost versus performance tradeoffs using the Embodiment Adaptation Curve (EAC) in your own robotics research and deployments.
limitations: The discussion focuses primarily on robotic manipulation (arms and end-effectors); extending the embodiment gap analysis to mobile robotics, such as legged locomotion, humanoid balancing, and rough-terrain navigation, remains future work.

Inter-rater agreement for the vertical axis (remaining work stage) of the two-axis map was modest ($\kappa = 0.33$), indicating subjective ambiguity when separating control interface alignment from contact/force control.

Because most existing papers do not report real-world adaptation effort (such as intervention counts or tuning hours), retrospectively filling out the proposed report card for older literature is difficult.
